newsitem.title: USA: President of now-private Connie Lee sees a niche.
newsitem.headline: President of now-private Connie Lee sees a niche.

text.p: Connie Lee Insurance Co, cut loose from its ties to the federal government last week, will remain a niche player in the business of insuring municipal bonds, the company's president said.

"You can either be a high volume, low value-added business, or you can be a lower volume, high value-added business," Oliver Sockwell, Connie Lee's president and chief executive officer, said in an interview with Reuters.

Sockwell said Connie Lee will continue to work on the smaller universe of deals that require more intensive structuring but reward insurers with higher premiums. Much of the rest of the industry, he said, tends to focus on the high-volume strategy of insuring relatively simple but lower premium issues.

President Clinton last week signed legislation expanding and deregulating Connie Lee, which was created by Congress in 1988 to insure lower-rated bonds issued by teaching hospitals and higher education institutions.
The new legislation requires the Department of Education to divest its 14 percent share in Connie Lee, and frees the company to begin moving into other market sectors.
But despite the government's official permission to expand, Sockwell said he has no plans to begin competing head-to-head with the industry's major players.
For the first half of 1996, Connie Lee applied its AAA rating to just $368 million of bonds. That compares to $17.6 billion for industry leader MBIA Insurance Corp, a unit of MBIA Inc.
"We expect to remain a relatively smaller company, a specialty company, more of a niche player," Sockwell said. "But we think there's plenty of opportunity out there without expanding too much."

Sockwell said specific details of the transition to a private company are still being worked out, and it would be premature to name new sectors or types of business Connie Lee would now pursue. He said decisions about those issues would likely be finalized early next year.

He also declined to say whether the company is in talks with Moody's Investors Service for a rating. Connie Lee is the only municipal bond insurer with a AAA from Standard & Poor's that does not also have a Moody's rating.
"We will consider whether another rating is appropriate as we move into new businesses," Sockwell said.

S&P affirmed its AAA grade after Clinton signed the privatization measure last week, saying that the removal of constraints on the company will increase diversity and "should better balance the risk profile of the company."

Sockwell stressed that the new Connie Lee would not resemble other small companies that have sought to gradually build themselves into direct competitors of MBIA and other dominant companies in the industry.

Capital Guaranty Insurance Co and Bond Investors Guaranty, for example, were smaller players that faced an uphill battle for the name recognition and market liquidity required to compete directly. Both were eventually swallowed up by other players.

"The secret of our success has always been remaining a company that is capitalized appropriately," Sockwell said. "We do not see our main business being a competitor of the largest companies for the market share that they currently have."
Richard Weill, MBIA's president, said he agreed with Sockwell's analysis of Connie Lee's position in the market.
"He's come up with a strategy that makes sense," Weill said in an interview. "In the short run, they don't have enough capital and enough personnel to effectively cover the entire market."

MBIA and other bond insurance firms previously opposed allowing Connie Lee to expand beyond its original Congressional mandate, arguing that Connie Lee's ties to the U.S. government imputed a federal guarantee to the bonds it insured.
But the industry supported an expansion if Connie Lee became fully private and its ties to the federal government severed, as in the legislation signed by Clinton last week.
"This is good government," Weill said of the privatization bill. "This is how it should have happened."
